Hard times

School bullying

What it is and is not, how to spot it, why it leaves a mark and what families and schools can do.

The Norwegian psychologist Dan Olweus, a pioneer in this field, defined bullying by three features: it is intentional, it is repeated over time and there is an imbalance of power between the person who bullies and the person who suffers it. A one-off fight between equals is not bullying; daily insults, systematic exclusion from the group, hitting, rumours or humiliation on social media are. A meta-analysis by Kelly Modecki estimated that around a third of adolescents are involved in traditional bullying, as victims or perpetrators, and about one in seven in cyberbullying.

Why it leaves a mark

Bullying is not "just kids being kids". William Copeland followed more than a thousand young people in North Carolina into adulthood and found that those who had been victims had more anxiety, depression and panic disorder as adults. Those who were both victims and bullies had the worst outcomes. Cyberbullying adds that there is no refuge: it follows them home, at night, on their phone.

Warning signs

Many children do not tell anyone, out of shame or fear of making things worse. It is worth noticing changes such as not wanting to go to school, stomach aches or headaches on school days, lost belongings or torn clothes, falling grades, poor sleep, withdrawing, deleting or hiding things on their phone, or having no one to meet up with.

The role of others

Bullying almost always happens in front of others. Programmes that work, such as Finland's KiVa, focus above all on bystanders: they teach children not to laugh along, to stand by the victim and to tell an adult. In schools that used it, bullying fell significantly.

What tends to help

  • Listening and believing. Thanking them for telling you, not minimising ("just ignore them") or blaming ("you must have done something").
  • Talking to the school. Schools generally have a duty to act on suspected bullying. Ask for a meeting with the form tutor or head and keep a written record.
  • Keeping evidence of cyberbullying: screenshots, dates, names.
  • Not confronting the child who bullies or their family directly: it usually makes things worse.
  • Specialist support. Many countries have free helplines for children and parents; in Spain, the ANAR Foundation answers on 900 20 20 10, free and 24 hours.

References

  1. Olweus, D. (1993). Bullying at School: What We Know and What We Can Do. Oxford: Blackwell. (Trad. cast.: Conductas de acoso y amenaza entre escolares, Morata, 1998).
  2. Modecki, K. L., Minchin, J., Harbaugh, A. G., Guerra, N. G. y Runions, K. C. (2014). Bullying prevalence across contexts: a meta-analysis measuring cyber and traditional bullying. Journal of Adolescent Health, 55(5), 602–611.
  3. Copeland, W. E., Wolke, D., Angold, A. y Costello, E. J. (2013). Adult psychiatric outcomes of bullying and being bullied by peers in childhood and adolescence. JAMA Psychiatry, 70(4), 419–426.
  4. Kärnä, A. et al. (2011). A large-scale evaluation of the KiVa antibullying program: grades 4–6. Child Development, 82(1), 311–330.
